GAD Antibody Positive
Paraneoplastic Stiff Person
Syndrome in a Patient with Renal
Cell Carcinoma
John C. McHugh, MRCPI, 1* Brian Murray, MD, 1
Radhakrishnan Renganathan, MRCPI, 1
Sean Connolly, FRCPI, 2 and Tim Lynch, FRCPI 1
1Department of Neurology, Mater Misericordiae University
Hospital, Dublin, Ireland; 2Department of Clinical
Neurophysiology, St Vincent’s University Hospital, Elm Park,
Dublin, Ireland
Abstract: Stiff person syndrome (SPS) is an unusual cause
of muscle rigidity and spasms. It is believed to have an
autoimmune pathogenesis and is associated with autoanti-
bodies to glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD). Paraneoplas-
tic SPS (PSPS) has been described mainly in relation to
breast cancer and is associated with antibodies to am-
phiphysin. Few reports of PSPS document the ﬁnding of
GAD autoantibodies. We present the ﬁrst reported case of
anti-GAD positive PSPS in a 53-year-old male with occult
renal carcinoma. Clinical beneﬁt was marked following
nephrectomy and intravenous immunoglobulin treatment.
Renal carcinoma should be considered in patients with SPS.
© 2007 Movement Disorder Society
Key words: stiff person syndrome; GAD; paraneoplastic;
IVIG.
Stiff person syndrome (SPS) is an uncommon CNS
disorder comprising stiffness and spasms of axial mus-
cles with continuous motor unit activation (CMUA), and
abnormal exteroceptive reﬂexes on EMG. Stiff limb syn-
drome (SLS) is a variant of SPS where symptoms are
disproportionate to a limb. It is believed that both disor-
ders share an autoimmune mechanism and there is a
strong association with autoantibodies to glutamic acid
decarboxylase (GAD).
1 A small proportion of cases are
considered to be paraneoplastic. The autoantibody to

amphiphysin was considered an important marker for
such cases, particularly in association with breast can-
cer.
2 More recently, however, a number of other antibod-
ies, including GAD, have been described in association
with paraneoplastic SPS (PSPS)/SLS and a variety of

positive SLS associated with a renal cell carcinoma.
CASE REPORT
A 53-year-old man with a history of Type 2 diabetes
and autoimmune hypothyroidism presented with an 11-
month history of pain and spasm in his left leg. He was
otherwise well. He ﬁrst noticed symptoms of minor
cramping in the left buttock after long car journeys. Over
months he developed episodes of shooting pain in his left
leg, which were followed by stiffening and involuntary
dorsiﬂexion of the left great toe, spreading to involve
anterior and posterior thigh muscles and lasting for 15
minutes. Spasms of the limb became more frequent and
were precipitated by movement, startle, and light touch.
The associated pain was severe and could last more than
1 hr requiring opiate analgesia from his primary care
physician. Benzodiazepines and baclofen did not signif-
icantly improve his symptoms.
Examination revealed a stiff, swollen, abnormally pos-
tured left lower limb. His left foot was ﬁxed in plantar-
ﬂexion at the ankle, and his leg was hyper-extended and
partially adducted at the hip. He could achieve only
minimal ﬂexion of his left knee. His gait was slow and
painful with circumduction of his left leg and plantar-
ﬂexion of the foot. Examination of both upper limbs and
right lower limb was normal, including deep tendon
reﬂexes. Plantars were ﬂexor bilaterally. Reﬂexes could
not be elicited in the stiff left leg but were seen to spread
to the right side. There was no involvement of axial
muscles of the thorax or abdomen. Sensory examination
was normal and there were no trophic changes in the
limb. A clinical diagnosis of SLS was made.
EMG studies demonstrated CMUA at rest in antago-
nist muscle groups in the left leg (Fig. 1). Spinal mag-
netic resonance imaging was normal. Serum autoanti-
bodies to GAD were positive at a titer of 5,682 U/mL
(normal reference 0 –1 U/mL). Antibodies to amphiphy-
sin were negative. Abdominal ultrasound was performed
to investigate swelling of the left lower limb. This re-
vealed a right-sided renal mass conﬁrmed to be a renal
cell carcinoma at nephrectomy. Post operatively the pa-
tient improved with diazepam 10 mg BD, baclofen 30
mg TDS, and intensive physiotherapy. Because of resid-
ual focal stiffness 1 month after surgery, he was also
treated with intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) 2 g/kg
divided over 5 days. IVIG was repeated monthly for 6
months and was associated with signiﬁcant improvement
in leg stiffness, spasms, and pain. At 4-years follow up
he is pain-free on baclofen and diazepam alone and can
jog short distances and ride a bicycle.
DISCUSSION
Our report is the ﬁrst to document a case of anti-
GAD positive PSLS with a renal cell carcinoma. Au-
toantibodies to GAD 65 are present in close to 80% of
patients with classic SPS.
3 To date, however, there are
only 6 reported cases of anti-GAD associated PSPS.
Three of these were breast cancers, one was a thy-
moma, and 2 were hematological malignancies (Table
1).
4-9 Unfortunately, tumor specimen was not retained
in this case and therefore could not be tested for GAD
expression.
Only a small proportion of SPS/SLS occur in the
setting of cancer but these can be indistinguishable from
idiopathic cases on clinical and electrodiagnostic
grounds. Prominent upper limb and trunk involvement
together with rapid progression and poor response to
benzodiazepines may serve as important red ﬂags for
paraneoplastic SPS/SLS

2,9-11,13,14 although notably our
patient presented with a more classical lower-half distri-
bution. Previously antibodies to amphiphysin were re-
garded as an important marker for cancer in SPS al-
though now several paraneoplastic cases have been
reported in association with other autoantibodies such as
GAD, Ri, and Gephyrin (Table 1).
13,14
It is therefore unclear which patients may have
cancer in SPS and furthermore it is uncertain what
investigations are appropriate to evaluate for occult
malignancy given the expanding range of tumors de-
scribed in relation to SPS (Table 1). Clearly a detailed
physical examination including breast exam is essen-
tial. Equally a comprehensive immunologic screen
should be sent which would ideally include immuno-

histochemistry as well as tests for the well-character-
ized onco-neural antibodies. In addition, we would
propose mammography in women and consideration
of CT chest and abdomen in the initial evaluation. The
role of FDG PET has been validated in other paraneo-
plastic syndromes as well as in SPS and its wider use
may be justiﬁed.
14
Management of the primary tumor is central to
neurological outcome in patients with paraneoplastic
diseases. Symptomatic treatment in SPS/SLS typically
involves benzodiazepines (Clonazepam, diazepam)
alone or in combination with antispastic drugs (ba-
clofen, tizanidine). Often the response in PSPS is
poorer than in idiopathic disease, and the use of cor-
ticosteroids has been more effective.
1 Other forms of
immunotherapy such as cyclophosphamide, plasma-
pheresis, and immunoadsorption have also been de-
scribed.
4,8,10,11 Steroids were avoided in our patient
because of his diabetes and IVIG was tried instead.
IVIG is the only modality that has proved beneﬁcial in
a blinded crossover study in GAD-associated idio-
pathic SPS.
15 To our knowledge it has only been used
in two other cases of PSPS. 8,12
Our patient showed an initial improvement follow-
ing tumor resection, which leads us to suggest that the
syndrome was paraneoplastic and not idiopathic auto-
immune SPS. Further improvement in function and
stiffness was observed over 6 months of IVIG therapy.
The sustained improvement achieved over 4 years
without maintenance immunotherapy also implies a
paraneoplastic etiology.
We conclude that renal cell carcinoma should be con-
sidered in the differential diagnosis of SPS and that IVIG
therapy may be an effective immunologic monotherapy
in these cases. Autoantibodies to GAD may be a marker
for paraneoplastic disease.

Deep Brain Stimulation in
Tourette’s Syndrome
Rizma Jalees Bajwa, MD,1 Alain J. de Lotbinie`re, MD,2,3
Robert A. King, MD,4 Bahman Jabbari, MD,1
Susan Quatrano,4 Kimberly Kunze, RN,2
Lawrence Scahill, MSN, MPH, PhD,4,5
and James F. Leckman, MD4*
1Department of Neurology, Yale University School of Medicine,
New Haven, Connecticut, USA; 2Department of Neurosurgery,
Yale University School of Medicine, New Haven, Connecticut,
USA; 3Northern Weschester Hospital Cancer Center, Mount
Kisco, New York, USA; 4Child Study Center, Yale University
School of Medicine, New Haven, Connecticut, USA; 5Yale
University School of Nursing, New Haven, Connecticut, USA
Abstract: A 48-year-old man with severe, lifelong Tourette’s
syndrome (TS) characterized by forceful self-injurious motor
tics and obsessive-compulsive disorder was treated with bilat-
eral deep brain stimulation (DBS). The decision to treat was
based on his progressive neurological impairment (left sided
weakness secondary to spinal cord injury) because of his
relentless, violent head jerks. Electrodes were implanted at the
level of the medial part of the thalamus (centromedian nu-
cleus, the substantia periventricularis, and the nucleus ventro-
oralis internus). DBS resulted in a substantial reduction of tics.
These data show that bilateral DBS of the thalamus can have
a good effect on severe tics in adult patients suffering from
intractable TS. © 2007 Movement Disorder Society
Key words: Tourette’s syndrome; deep brain stimulation;
midline thalamic nuclei
Tourette’s syndrome (TS) is a chronic neuropsychiat-
ric disorder with onset in early childhood and character-
ized by motor and phonic tics. Tics are repetitive muscle
contractions that produce stereotyped movements (motor
tics) or sounds (phonic tics). Tics are often preceded by
subtle, seemingly irresistible sensory urges that are mo-
mentarily relieved with the performance of the tic. Co-
occurring disorders of attention and impulse control are
common, including attention-deﬁcit hyperactivity disor-
der (ADHD) and obsessive-compulsive disorder
(OCD).
1 Although TS is frequently self-limiting with tic
severity peaking early in the second decade of life, a
small fraction of patients go on to have severe tics during
adulthood.
2 Some of these cases result in self-injury,
because of recurrent hitting, biting, and cervical spine
damage injury due to violent head jerks. The standard
treatment is pharmacological, mainly involving neuro-
leptic medications, /H92512-adrenergic agonists, and dopa-
mine agonists as well as local injections of botulinum
toxin.
3 Behavioral treatment using techniques such as
habit reversal has been shown to be effective as well. 4 In
a small percentage of cases, however, symptoms are
refractory to these treatments. Since 1955, various at-
tempts have been made to treat these patients through
neurosurgical procedures with the most promising being

bilateral ablation of midline thalamic nuclei.
5 In 1999,
deep brain stimulation (DBS) was introduced as a new
approach for intractable TS. To date, ﬁve patients have
been reported who have undergone bilateral thalamic
stimulation with promising results on tics and associated
behavioral disorders.
6-8 Two other targets have also been
used: posteroventral globus pallidus internus (GPi) 7-9
and anterior limb of the internal capsule. 10 In the present
study, we report on the effects over 25 months of bilat-
eral thalamic stimulation in one patient with severe,
refractory TS.
PATIENTS AND METHODS
Case Report
This 50-year-old, left-handed man has had a severe,
life long course of TS beginning at the age of 3 years. He
had facial, head and neck, and vocal tics. His facial tics
primarily comprised increased blinking. His vocal tics
included grunting, loud noises, and cursing at times. He
was diagnosed with TS at the age of 13 years. He was
started on haloperidol at an average daily dose of 6 to 10
mg. He was trained as an emergency medical technician
and was able to work full time despite his tics. In 1976,
he participated in trials of a number of other medications
including a formal clozapine trial at NIH in an attempt to
control his tics.
11 Despite all the efforts, his tics gradually
worsened and became self injurious.
